q: Who is the author of the chapter "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
e: The author of the chapter "Lakhnavi Andaaz" is the renowned story writer and satirist Yashpal.

q: Which literary genre does "Lakhnavi Andaaz" belong to?
e: "Lakhnavi Andaaz" is a satirical work that mocks the false pride of the declining feudal class.

q: Which class ticket did the author buy on the train?
e: The author bought a Second Class ticket to save money while getting solitude to think.

q: Which train did the author have to travel by?
e: At the beginning of the chapter, it is stated that the mufassil passenger train was hissing eagerly to depart.

q: In what posture was the Nawab Sahib sitting on the compartment berth?
e: A respectable gentleman of Lucknowi aristocratic descent was sitting very comfortably cross-legged.

q: What was placed on the towel in front of Nawab Sahib?
e: Two fresh, shiny cucumbers were placed on a towel in front of Nawab Sahib.

q: Why had the author bought a Second Class ticket?
o: To think about a new story and watch natural scenery from the window
e: The author thought Second Class would be less crowded so he could think about a new story in solitude and enjoy the scenery.

q: What greeting did Nawab Sahib first offer upon addressing the author?
e: After pondering for a while, Nawab Sahib addressed the author saying, "Aadaab-arz, sir, would you care to enjoy some cucumber?"

q: What expression appeared in Nawab Sahib’s eyes when the author entered the compartment?
o: Dissatisfaction at the disturbance in his solitary contemplation
e: When the author suddenly hopped in, Nawab Sahib’s eyes showed dissatisfaction at the interruption of his solitary thoughts.

q: Considering cucumber what kind of item did the author guess the reason for Nawab Sahib’s hesitation?
e: The author thought Nawab Sahib felt awkward being seen enjoying a trivial item like a cucumber.

q: What did Nawab Sahib pick up from under the seat to wash the cucumbers?
e: Nawab Sahib picked up a lota from under the seat and washed both cucumbers outside the window.

q: Why did Nawab Sahib cut the ends of the cucumbers and prick them?
e: He cut the tips of both cucumbers and pricked them to draw out the bitter froth.

q: What did Nawab Sahib sprinkle on the cucumber slices?
o: Cumin-mixed salt and red chilli powder
e: Nawab Sahib neatly sprinkled cumin-mixed salt and red chilli powder onto the cucumber slices.

q: What do cucumber vendors at Lucknow station offer in a small paper packet to customers?
o: Cumin-mixed salt and ground red chilli
e: According to the text, cucumber vendors at Lucknow station also provide a small packet of cumin-mixed salt and ground red chilli.

q: Which special variety of cucumber did Nawab Sahib name?
e: Nawab Sahib told the author, "By God, please try it, it is Lucknow’s Balam cucumber!"

q: What reason did the author give when refusing the cucumber the second time?
o: He does not feel the urge right now and his stomach is a bit weak
e: Maintaining his self-respect, the author replied, "Thank you, I don’t feel the urge right now, and my stomach is also a bit weak."

q: What did Nawab Sahib ultimately do with the cucumber slices?
o: Smelled them and threw them out of the window
Put them in the author’s bag
e: Nawab Sahib brought each slice near his lips, smelled it, savoured its aroma in imagination, and tossed it out of the window.

q: What did Nawab Sahib do after throwing all the slices outside?
o: Wiped his hands and lips with the towel and lay down exhausted
e: Nawab Sahib wiped his hands and lips with the towel, looked proudly at the author, and lay down tired from the preparation.

q: What sound came from Nawab Sahib shortly after he lay down?
o: Of a loud belch from a full stomach
e: The sound of a loud belch, as if from a full stomach, was heard from Nawab Sahib.

q: What did Nawab Sahib say about cucumber after belching?
o: Cucumber should only be eaten in the morning
Cucumber is delicious but heavy to digest, it burdens the stomach
e: Nawab Sahib remarked, "Cucumber is delicious, yet it is heavy (sakeel); the wretched thing puts a burden on the stomach."

q: What does the word "Meda" mean in the chapter "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
e: The Urdu word "Meda" means stomach or digestive organ.

q: What is the correct meaning of the word "Sakeel"?
e: "Sakeel" means heavy or difficult to digest.

q: Based on which habit did the author try to guess what was in Nawab Sahib’s mind?
o: Old habit of sitting idle and imagining things
e: The author mentions his old habit of sitting idle and imagining things, which led him to guess Nawab Sahib’s discomfort.

q: How did the author respond mentally when Nawab Sahib smelled and threw away the cucumber?
o: He had to bow his head in acknowledgement (tasleem)
e: Seeing Nawab Sahib’s pride, the author sarcastically had to bow his head in acknowledgement (tasleem).

q: Which literary trend did the author satirize at the end of the chapter?
e: At the end, the author satirizes writers of "Nayi Kahani" who claim to write stories without thought, plot, or characters.

q: In which year and where was Yashpal born?
e: Yashpal was born in 1903 at Ferozepur Cantonment in Punjab.

q: What did the author assume the Second Class compartment would be like?
e: The author hurried into the Second Class compartment thinking it was empty, though contrary to his guess it was not.

q: What is meant by the term "Mufassil"?
o: Main market of a capital city
Suburban/outlying areas around a central town
e: According to NCERT glossary, "Mufassil" refers to the outlying places around a central city.

q: What did Nawab Sahib take out of his pocket to peel the cucumbers?
e: Nawab Sahib took out a knife from his pocket, cut the ends of both cucumbers, and peeled them.

q: Why did the author refuse the watery salted cucumber slices even though his mouth watered?
o: He forgot how to eat cucumber
He had already refused earlier, so he felt it right to uphold his self-respect
Nawab Sahib offered too few slices
e: Since the author had already declined once, he felt it appropriate to maintain his self-respect when asked again.

q: What was the initial behaviour between the author and Nawab Sahib?
o: Both avoided eye contact and remained silent
Nawab Sahib forced the author off
e: Since Nawab Sahib showed no enthusiasm for company, the author too sat opposite and averted his eyes out of self-respect.

q: What probable reason did the author imagine for Nawab Sahib travelling in Second Class?
o: He was going to meet a poor friend
Bought out of thriftiness assuming he could travel completely alone
e: The author guessed that he bought Second Class for economy assuming solitude, and now felt embarrassed in front of another gentleman.

q: Which social group does the word "Safedposh" symbolize in the chapter?
o: Respectable, status-conscious gentry concerned with outward appearances
e: "Safedposh" means a respectable gentleman who worries about maintaining social prestige and outward dignity.

q: Why did Nawab Sahib go through such a long and meticulous preparation for the cucumbers?
o: He was taking a culinary exam
To display his aristocratic refinement, delicacy, and elite manners
To wait for the train to halt
e: Spreading the towel, washing, removing froth, and arranging slices were all part of his aristocratic etiquette and pretentious display.

q: How was Nawab Sahib’s anticipation of relishing the cucumber visible on his face?
o: He was shaking his head repeatedly
Every facial gesture and twitching of jaws showed his mouth watering in anticipation
e: The twitching of his jaws and his expressions clearly showed his mouth filling with water at the thought of tasting it.

q: Why did the author dislike Nawab Sahib’s sudden change of attitude?
o: The author sensed he wanted to drag him into ordinary behaviour just to keep up his own show of gentility
e: When Nawab Sahib suddenly greeted and offered cucumber, the author realized it was merely an empty formality to preserve his gentlemanly image.

q: What does the idiom "kankhiyon se dekhna" mean in the context of the chapter?
o: Looking sideways discreetly / out of the corner of one’s eye
e: Instead of staring directly, the author observed Nawab Sahib’s actions discreetly out of the corner of his eye.

q: How did Nawab Sahib react while smelling the slice of cucumber?
o: Closed his eyes in bliss of taste and swallowed the saliva that filled his mouth
Put the slice back on the towel
e: On smelling the slice, his eyelids closed in sheer sensory pleasure and he swallowed the mouthful of saliva.

q: According to the author, what method of consuming cucumbers did Nawab Sahib adopt?
o: A subtle, refined, or abstract method of satisfaction through aroma and imagination
e: The author calls it a subtle, refined, or abstract way of feeling satisfied merely by the aroma and imagination of taste.

q: What key question arose in the author’s mind regarding this abstract way of eating?
o: Does it make the cucumber sweeter?
Is doing this on a train legal?
Can such a method actually satisfy the hunger of the stomach?
e: The author wondered whether such an abstract method could truly satisfy the stomach’s hunger.

q: Why did the author’s "eyes of knowledge" (gyan-chakshu) open after Nawab Sahib belched?
o: He realized that just like getting full by smell, "Nayi Kahani" is claimed to be written without plot, thought, or characters
He saw the next railway station
He discovered Nawab Sahib’s real name
e: If imagining a cucumber’s taste can produce a full-stomach belch, then a "New Story" can similarly be claimed without plot, characters, or thought.

q: Which of the following works is NOT authored by Yashpal?
e: "Aapka Bunty" is a famous novel by Mannu Bhandari, whereas "Jhootha Sach", "Dada Comrade", and "Divya" are by Yashpal.

q: Which act of Nawab Sahib did the author sarcastically label as "aristocratic etiquette, refinement, and delicacy"?
o: Smelling the cucumber slices, throwing them out, and lying down exhausted
e: The author made this ironic remark on the drama of smelling and discarding the cucumber and then lying down exhausted.

q: What does "Lakhnavi Andaaz" primarily critique?
o: The artificial lifestyle and pretentiousness of the declining feudal class
e: Yashpal wrote this satire targeting the decaying feudal class that clings to an artificial lifestyle detached from reality.

q: What did Nawab Sahib do while looking out of the window before throwing the cucumber?
e: Nawab Sahib looked longingly at the cucumber slices and took a deep sigh while looking out of the window.

q: What thought crossed the author’s mind regarding Nawab Sahib’s "aristocratic status" while watching him prepare the cucumber?
o: He poses as an aristocrat, yet thinking he is unobserved, he has come down to his real ordinary tastes
He is a very miserly merchant
e: Watching him peel and season the cucumber, the author thought the gentleman had dropped his aristocratic pretence thinking no acquaintance was watching.

q: What mentality is reflected in Nawab Sahib’s hesitation over buying and eating cucumbers?
o: Pressure of false social status and outward show
e: He feared that eating a common item like cucumber in front of another gentleman would diminish his aristocratic dignity.

q: What does the word "Surkhi" mean in the chapter?
e: "Laal mirch ki surkhi" refers to the red powder of ground chillies.

q: What does Yashpal imply by referring to the writers of "Nayi Kahani"?
o: Writers claiming to write stories through pure abstraction without plot, events, or characters
e: Yashpal uses "Nayi Kahani" to satirize the tendency of writing contentless literature disconnected from real life.

q: With which words did Nawab Sahib invite the author a second time to eat the cucumber?
o: Take it, at least eat a little.
By God, please try it, it is Lucknow’s Balam cucumber!
This cucumber is very expensive, eat it.
Eat it for yourself if not for me.
e: After seasoning the slices, Nawab Sahib proudly said, "By God, please try it, it is Lucknow’s Balam cucumber!"

q: What did the author say when declining the cucumber for the first time?
o: Thank you, sir (Qibla), please enjoy it yourself.
e: Responding with equal formality, the author politely said, "Thank you, sir, please enjoy it yourself."

q: When is the conflict between the "real and artificial" visible in Nawab Sahib’s behaviour?
o: When he does not speak to the author
When he gets off the train
When his mouth waters for the cucumber, yet he throws it away uneaten to display aristocracy
e: His intense inner craving (mouth watering) versus outwardly throwing the slices away reveals the clash between reality and pretence.

q: What is the prominent feature of the language and style of "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: Standard Khadi Boli Hindi with apt, satirical use of Urdu-Persian and English words
e: Yashpal blends Urdu terms (aadaab, talab, meda, nafaasat) and English words (second class, abstract) seamlessly into Hindi to evoke Lucknowi culture.

q: What is the meaning of "Satrishna aankhon"?
o: Eyes filled with thirst or longing/craving
e: "Satrishna" means filled with desire or longing; Nawab Sahib looked at the glistening slices with craving eyes.

q: Where did Nawab Sahib neatly arrange each slice of the cucumber?
e: He shook out the towel kept beneath the cucumbers, spread it in front, and neatly arranged the slices on it.

q: What does the word "Gumaan" indicate in the context of this chapter?
e: In "sharaafat ka gumaan banaye rakhne ke liye", "gumaan" implies maintaining an illusion or pride of gentility.

q: Which social flaw is exposed by Nawab Sahib’s behaviour with an ordinary item like a cucumber?
e: Throwing away perfectly edible cucumber merely to show off aristocracy highlights false ostentation and wastefulness.

q: Wherein lies the appropriateness of the title "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: It centers on the artificial delicacy, refinement, and showy etiquette of Lucknowi aristocrats
It describes historical monuments of Lucknow
The author himself hailed from Lucknow
e: The entire satire revolves around the artificial etiquette and affected mannerisms of a Lucknowi Nawab, making the title apt.

q: What assumption did the author make before boarding Second Class that turned out to be wrong?
o: That the ticket would be very cheap
That the compartment would be completely deserted
That the compartment would have AC
e: The author assumed the Second Class compartment would be empty, yet a Nawab Sahib was already seated inside.

q: Which literary ideology did Yashpal represent in Hindi literature?
e: Yashpal was a progressive, realistic writer who attacked social hypocrisy and class divisions.

q: Context: "Our sudden hopping into the compartment caused dissatisfaction in the gentleman’s eyes at the interruption of his solitary contemplation." — What was the real cause behind this discomfort?
o: Nawab Sahib felt awkward about being seen with ordinary cucumbers while pretending high aristocracy
Nawab Sahib was composing a serious poem
e: The "solitary contemplation" was a facade; in reality, he did not want another gentleman to catch him eating cucumbers in Second Class.

q: If Nawab Sahib had actually eaten the cucumber, which aspect of his projected persona would have been affected?
o: In his own eyes, the illusion of his aristocratic refinement and fastidiousness would shatter
e: Eating it would make him look like an ordinary person; discarding it untouched sustained his illusion of being extraordinary.

q: In today’s context, if someone takes loans to host lavish showy events, which aspect of the chapter does it resemble?
o: The author buying a Second Class ticket
Nawab Sahib smelling and throwing away the cucumber to uphold declining feudal pride
e: Indulging in wasteful show-off for false prestige despite lacking real substance parallels Nawab Sahib’s mentality.

q: Context: "This is the way of ancestral aristocrats!" — Identify the irony embedded in this line.
o: Throwing food away after smelling it is not true nobility, but ridiculous pretension detached from reality
e: Under the guise of praising aristocracy, the line sharply mocks its hollow, impractical pretension.

q: How did the author see himself and Nawab Sahib mirroring each other in the compartment?
o: Both remained formal and restrained out of gentlemanly ego and self-respect
Both belonged to the same village
e: While Nawab Sahib clung to aristocratic pride, the author too refused the cucumber despite craving it, just to guard his self-respect.

q: In "the wretched thing puts a burden on the stomach", what psychological defence is Nawab Sahib using?
o: Inventing an excuse to justify his fake satisfaction and superior status without eating
Scaring the author away from cucumbers
Asking for a cure for his illness
e: To disguise the absurdity of discarding the cucumber, he calls it "heavy" as if he had actually eaten and digested it.

q: Why did the author describe the "lota", "knife", "towel", and "salt-chilli" in such meticulous detail?
o: To show cleanliness of the train
To heighten the contrast between the elaborate ritualistic build-up and its hollow, absurd climax
To make an inventory of items
e: The more elaborate and serious the preparation, the more absurd and satirical the final act of throwing the slices out becomes.

q: Context: If a belch can come from imagining cucumber, why can’t a New Story be made without thought, event, and characters? — What does "cucumber" symbolize here?
o: The concrete substance of a story (thought, plot/events, and characters)
e: Just as solid food (cucumber) is needed to actually satisfy hunger, concrete ideas, events, and characters are needed for a meaningful story.

q: Observing what state of Nawab Sahib did the author wonder if he too was worried about finding a story idea?
o: When he sat alone looking out the window in a posture of deep contemplation
When he was reading a book
When he was talking to the ticket collector
e: Since the author himself boarded Second Class to think of a story, seeing Nawab Sahib’s pensive look made him project the same motive onto him.

q: Both the author and Nawab Sahib chose Second Class, yet what was the difference in their motives?
o: Author wanted crowd, Nawab wanted noise
Author sought affordable creative solitude; Nawab sought economy while hiding his reduced status from acquaintances
Nawab Sahib did not know the route
e: The author boarded for creative solitude within a budget, while Nawab Sahib wanted to save money without letting peers see him travel in a lower class.

q: What natural human reaction did the author show when Nawab Sahib sprinkled salt and chilli on the cucumbers?
o: His mouth watered at the sight of the juicy seasoned slices
e: The author’s mouth watering at the glistening, salted cucumber slices was a completely natural human reaction.

q: How does the conflict of "reality vs imagination" help understand Nawab Sahib’s character?
o: He was narrating a children’s tale
He was travelling in a dream
He rejected real appetite and taste, pretending satisfaction through imagined flavour alone
e: His entire class, detached from present reality, lives in an illusion of past grandeur and imagined satisfaction.

q: If the story had ended with Nawab Sahib eating the cucumber, how would it affect the central satire?
o: The satire on hollow feudal pretension and contentless "Nayi Kahani" would be lost
e: Smelling, discarding, and then belching is the backbone of the satire that exposes the absurdity of hollow pretension.

q: In "a respectable gentleman... sitting very comfortably cross-legged", what mentality does this posture signify?
o: Sense of entitlement, ease, and aristocratic poise
e: Sitting cross-legged at complete ease across the berth reflects aristocratic entitlement and poise.

q: Which sensory imagery is evoked by "watery cucumber slices" (paniyati phanken) in the text?
o: Gustatory and visual imagery (taste and sight)
e: The description of glistening, juicy slices dusted with salt and chilli vividly stimulates visual and gustatory senses.

q: The author sat opposite and "averted his eyes out of self-respect" — what trait of the author does this reveal?
o: Self-dignity and refusal to beg for unwanted attention
e: When the co-passenger showed no warmth, the author upheld his dignity by not forcing interaction.

q: What irony is highlighted by Nawab Sahib "lying down exhausted" after the cucumber episode?
o: Performing needless formalities and pretension exhausts a person over nothing productive
Cutting cucumber is the hardest labour
The train berth was too comfortable
e: Getting exhausted merely from preparing and smelling without eating exposes the sheer futility of pretension.

q: Context: "Thank you, I don’t feel the urge right now..." — Why did the author use Urdu vocabulary in this dialogue?
o: To respond politely and ironically in the same refined Lucknowi linguistic register as Nawab Sahib
e: By using words like "talab", "meda", and "qibla", the author matched Nawab Sahib’s Lucknowi register with polite irony.

q: What reality is depicted by mentioning the cucumber sellers of "Lucknow station" in the chapter?
o: Only cucumbers are sold in Lucknow
The practical know-how and grounded service of ordinary vendors, contrasting with the Nawab’s artificiality
The train halts there for two hours
e: Station vendors understand practical taste and utility (offering seasoned salt packets), contrasting with the Nawab’s empty show.

q: Which poetic/literary device is visible in "the mufassil passenger train was hissing in eagerness to start"?
e: Attributing human-like eagerness ("utavali") to a non-living train makes it an instance of personification.

q: If a student feels satisfied merely by imagining high marks without studying, which character does the student resemble?
o: Nawab Sahib who belches merely by smelling the cucumber
e: Just as Nawab Sahib claims fullness through imagination without eating, expecting results without real effort mirrors his delusion.

q: What is meant by Nawab Sahib relishing the cucumber "with vaasna" (Vaasna se rasaasvaadan)?
o: Experiencing the flavour mentally through aroma and intense longing
e: Here "vaasna" refers to inhaling the fragrance and savouring it through intense desire.

q: Which action of Nawab Sahib did the author interpret as "coming down to his real self"?
o: When he spread the towel and started washing, peeling, and seasoning the cucumber like ordinary people
e: The author assumed that believing himself unseen by peers, the Nawab was giving in to the ordinary human urge to eat cucumber.

q: Of which historical-social transition does Nawab Sahib appear to be a relic/victim in the chapter?
o: Unemployment due to spread of education
Inability to let go of feudal arrogance even after the decline of the feudal system
e: Clinging to aristocratic airs even while reduced to Second Class travel reflects the decay of feudalism.

q: Which trait of the author is reflected in his decision to board a Second Class compartment?
o: Practicality and economy combined with a desire for creative reflection
e: Since the journey wasn’t long, he made a practical choice to save money while getting quiet space to think of a story.

q: How was Nawab Sahib’s demeanour during the "preparation of the cucumbers"?
e: Spreading the towel, pricking for froth, peeling carefully, and arranging slices neatly show utmost poise and orderliness.

q: Which incident likely inspired the author to write this chapter?
o: The bizarre train encounter with a pretentious Nawab who smelled, threw away cucumbers, and then belched
High price of salt and chilli
e: The Nawab’s bizarre behaviour in the train gave Yashpal material to satirize both feudal hypocrisy and abstract story writing.

q: “Wiped his hands and lips with the towel” — What does wiping lips without eating prove?
o: He wanted to wash his face
He wanted to play out his aristocratic charade down to the smallest realistic detail
e: Wiping his lips despite eating nothing proves how thoroughly he was acting out his aristocratic charade.

q: What practical message about life does the reader get from Yashpal’s chapter?
o: One should avoid false show and ostentation and live realistically with simplicity
One should travel only in First Class
One should never talk while travelling
e: The chapter teaches that authenticity and realism, rather than empty show, form the basis of a meaningful life.

q: Why did the author choose the example of a "belch" to mock "Nayi Kahani"?
o: To show how ridiculous it is to claim satisfaction/a story without solid substance (food/plot)
Because he liked the sound of a belch
e: Claiming a full-stomach belch without eating is as absurd as claiming a story without ideas, events, or characters.

q: “Had to bow my head in tasleem” — Is the author’s gesture here genuine reverence or satirical irony?

q: What kind of structural irony does Nawab Sahib’s act of smelling, discarding, and then belching create in the text?
o: Complete incongruity between cause and effect (claiming effect without cause)
e: Belching (effect) without eating (cause) violates real-world logic, forming the structural core of the satire.

q: In this chapter, "Lucknow" transcends geography to signify which cultural connotation?
o: The tradition of aristocratic etiquette (tehzeeb), delicacy, and decadent feudal show-off
e: Lucknow is historically tied to courtly etiquette and refinement, whose decayed, pretentious form is spotlighted here.

q: While explaining his Second Class choice, the author notes "to avoid spending too much" — what is its significance for the narrative?

q: What subtle parallel did Yashpal draw between the "Nayi Kahani writer" and "Nawab Sahib"?
o: Both claim creation/fulfilment purely through abstraction without concrete reality (food / plot-characters)
e: As a realist, Yashpal equates plotless writing with the Nawab’s imaginary belch—both lack concrete substance.

q: “He swallowed the mouthful of saliva that filled his mouth” — What inner truth about Nawab Sahib does this line expose?
o: His natural body and senses craved real food, yet false ego stopped him from eating it
e: It exposes the absurdity of suppressing genuine biological desire merely to satisfy false social pride.

q: What literary effect is achieved by the presence of words like "Aadaab-arz", "Qibla", "Wallah", and "Namuraad"?

It creates an authentic cultural atmosphere of Lucknow and sharpens the satirical edge
e: Adapting vocabulary to character and setting creates an authentic Lucknowi ambience that makes the satire crisp and natural.

q: What would change if the title "Lakhnavi Andaaz" were replaced by "Khokhli Nawabi" (Hollow Aristocracy)?
o: The satire would become blunt and flat, whereas "Lakhnavi Andaaz" preserves subtle irony and cultural nuance
e: "Lakhnavi Andaaz" sounds complimentary on the surface while concealing biting irony—the hallmark of refined satire.

q: In what dual context does the concept of "story" (kahani) appear in this chapter?
o: Initially as the author’s motive to think of a new story, and finally as a satirical conclusion on "Nayi Kahani"
Only as Nawab Sahib’s childhood story
The word does not appear in the chapter
e: The chapter opens with the author seeking a story idea and closes with a satirical revelation about the "Nayi Kahani" trend itself.

q: Which human limitation or vulnerability of the author himself also surfaces in "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: Declining something he genuinely craved (mouth watering) out of rigid formality and pride
e: Not just the Nawab, even the author suppresses his genuine craving due to gentlemanly pride—a subtle portrayal of human nature.

q: Which statement most accurately captures the central theme of the chapter?
o: One should not accept cucumbers from strangers on trains
Second Class travel is always painful
Both an artificial lifestyle divorced from reality and substance-free literary posing are futile and laughable
e: Through the Nawab, Yashpal exposes the futility of both social pretension in life and empty formalism in literature.

q: In Nawab Sahib’s context, taking a "deep sigh" (deergh nishwas) indicates which state of mind?
o: Helplessness at not being able to eat, nostalgia for lost grandeur, and staging fake detachment
e: Sighing deeply before tossing away what he craved reveals both internal restraint and theatrical gravity.

q: Based on the chapter, what was the key occurrence that went "contrary to expectation" (anumaan ke pratikool)?
o: The Second Class compartment not being empty and having Nawab Sahib inside
e: The author boarded expecting solitude, but contrary to his assumption, an aristocratic gentleman was already seated there.

q: What social division is indicated in the chapter by contrasting "ancestral aristocrats" and "ordinary people"?
o: Feudal class stratification and an arrogant superiority complex
e: Nawab Sahib strives through every gesture to mark himself superior to commoners, reflecting entrenched class consciousness.

q: What kind of descriptive style has Yashpal employed in "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: First-person narrative ("I/We") with keen psychological observation and satire
e: Using first-person narration, Yashpal keenly observes and satirizes every micro-gesture and psychological shift of the Nawab.

q: In what tone is the word "Qibla" used in "Shukriya, Qibla shauk farmaayein"?
o: Hyper-polite formal respect carrying a subtle undercurrent of irony
e: "Qibla" is a respectful Urdu honorific; the author matches the Nawab’s formal delicacy with poised politeness.

q: Was Nawab Sahib genuinely wealthy or was his aristocracy merely a vestige of the past? What does the text suggest?

q: How does Nawab Sahib’s "abstract" consumption of cucumber connect to modern show-off/consumerist culture?
o: Even today many prioritize status symbols, image, and wasteful display over genuine utility and joy
e: Sacrificing genuine utility and joy while wasting resources for social image mirrors contemporary status-driven ostentation.

q: From an examination perspective, which is the best example of "symbolism" in "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: Belching from cucumber aroma = writing Nayi Kahani without plot or characters
e: The episode transforms into a literary symbol where cucumber stands for solid content and the belch stands for illusory artistic fulfilment.

e: Nawab shows dissatisfaction/hesitation upon entry, the author upholds self-respect in refusing, and Nawab concludes with proud display.

q: “A person detached from reality ultimately becomes a figure of ridicule” — To which scene does this apply most accurately?

Buying a ticket at the station

Looking at scenery from the window

q: What is the purpose of satire in Yashpal’s writing, as seen in "Lakhnavi Andaaz"?
o: Exposing social hypocrisy, class ego, and unreal tendencies to steer society toward realism
e: Yashpal’s satire is not mere comedy; it aims to expose social hypocrisy and awaken realistic consciousness.

q: “He kept looking out the window pondering the situation” — What is the psychological analysis of this action by Nawab Sahib?
o: He was devising a strategy to handle the cucumbers while preserving his prestige in front of a gentleman

e: The author’s sudden presence put him in a dilemma; gazing outside gave him time to plan how to save his aristocratic image.

q: Why is "Lakhnavi Andaaz" often described as a reflective satirical sketch/story?

Because it is written in verse
e: It combines a train incident with reflective commentary on feudal culture and literary trends.

q: Nawab Sahib had two cucumbers yet ate none—what attitude toward wastefulness (apavyaya) emerges from this episode?

A culture of ostentation senselessly destroys useful resources and food, which is socially unjustifiable
e: Throwing away edible food merely for egoistic display sharply critiques pointless extravagance and waste.

q: What contrasting situations are shown by "looking out of the corner of the eye" and "averting eyes" in the text?

e: Out of dignity the author avoids forced interaction, yet as a keen writer he quietly observes every detail of Nawab Sahib’s behaviour.

q: Regarding "Nayi Kahani", the author’s final question—"Why can’t it be made?"—is an example of which rhetorical device?
o: Rhetorical irony (whose implied real answer is that a meaningful story cannot exist without substance)
e: This rhetorical question ironically asserts the opposite: that a true story cannot be written without thought, plot, and characters.

q: Based on "Lakhnavi Andaaz", what is the greatest irony of a declining privileged class?
o: They have too much free time
Instead of accepting changed reality, they cling to hollow ego and showy rituals
e: Clinging to a shell of aristocratic grandeur despite altered material reality is the central irony of a decaying feudal class.
